summary_pt: Entreguei a seção (inglês, ~4.100 palavras, com versão curta indicada), 65 entradas BibTeX e um log de verificação (referência -> URL aberta -> o que foi checado -> profundidade de leitura). Todas as 65 foram resolvidas por Crossref, API do arXiv ou página aberta, e o log registra onde só li abstract ou metadado. Achado principal: o arXiv 2610.02070 (Behnam & Wang, 1 out 2026, "Causal Memory Policy") randomiza slots de recuperação com propensidades conhecidas e formaliza a "violação de positividade" no nível da recuperação. É exatamente o modo de falha do nosso §3.0.1, em que o boost é endereçado por id e os chunks saem da lista de candidatos, então tratamento e controle viram a mesma intervenção em 214 de 234 epochs. A seção posiciona o ensaio contra esse trabalho sem afirmar prioridade, e diz o que o ensaio não faz: não identifica utilidade por memória, não randomiza dentro do brief, não faz interleaving, não estima carryover, não mede custo e compara duas políticas, não memória contra ausência de memória. O §9.6 do survey TMLR é vizinho do nosso desenho, não instância: ele pede comparar agentes com memória contra baselines sem memória, e nós comparamos dois políticas de uma memória sempre ligada. Contei as strings no PDF fixado por sha256 (497e9549...): zero "random*" e zero "pre-regist*"; "A/B" aparece uma vez, como custo que simuladores poupam. Omri et al. medem custo por fase (tokens, latência, energia) sem contraste randomizado, e nosso manuscrito não mede custo. A busca não achou nenhum ensaio pré-registrado randomizado de memória em tráfego real, nem trilha de registered reports em IR; só o design de seis gates de Feng et al., em benchmark. A seção declara essa busca como limitada e feita por um agente só. Lacunas: nenhum livro foi aberto (Kohavi, Imbens-Rubin; a página da Cambridge deu 429), e vários artigos pagos só têm metadado. Não reli o MemoryArena v2 (17/set) em texto integral; só busquei strings, e a leitura integral de 15/ago foi de versão anterior. Não rodei git, não editei arquivo existente, e não toquei nas VPS.

proposed_text_en:
TARGET: new section "## 8. Related work" in MANUSCRIPT-B.md, placed before the current "## 8. Discussion" (renumber Discussion to 9 and update cross-references). Citation keys resolve in _sprint-2026-10-04/B-related-work.bib; the full long form is B-related-work.md. Condensed insert:

## 8. Related work

We read each body of work for what it gives us and for what this trial does not do that its authors do. Paper A (section 8) covers the exposure and surface literature and is not repeated.

**Agent-memory evaluation.** Benchmarks compare systems on fixed task suites [@he2026memoryarena; @wei2025evomemory; @zheng2025lifelongagentbench; @hu2025memoryagentbench; @maharana2024locomo; @wu2025longmemeval; @zou2026interruptbench]. Evo-Memory fixes task order as a fairness device and itself reports that order matters (ExpRAG average success 0.57 under Easy-to-Hard versus 0.69 under Hard-to-Easy), but compares two sorted orders, not sampled ones. The TMLR survey [@huang2026survey] asks in section 9.6 for "closed-loop, longitudinal, and execution-grounded evaluation paradigms" that compare "memory-augmented agents and memory-free baselines under identical conditions". This trial is a neighbour of that direction, not an instance: it contrasts two policies of an always-on memory, not memory against none. On the pinned PDF the survey contains no occurrence of "random*" or "pre-regist*", and "A/B" appears once, as a cost that user simulators spare; we read this as the absence of a convention, not as a claim that nobody has run such experiments. Omri et al. [@omri2026agentmemory] attribute tokens, latency and energy to construction, retrieval and generation across ten systems, with no randomised contrast; we report no cost, latency or energy.

**Interventional studies of memory.** The nearest work is Behnam and Wang [@behnam2026cmp] (arXiv, 1 Oct 2026), who show that a memory's utility is not identified by any design that randomises only its inclusion when it is not retrievable (a retrieval-level positivity violation), and restore identification by randomising which memories fill k reserved context slots with known propensities. Our section 3.0.1 documents an instance of that failure on live traffic: the boost is addressed by id, the designated chunks leave the candidate list, and treatment and control become the same intervention for 214 of 234 registered epochs. We had no such framing at registration (2026-08-18) and claim no priority. The designs differ in estimand (their per-memory utility per interaction; our intention-to-treat effect of one lever with the fleet epoch as unit), in setting (their benchmarks and a Mem0 replay; our live fleet) and in registration (ours is pre-registered; theirs, as far as we read, is not). We do not identify individual memory utility, do not randomise within a brief, and have no propensity-weighted estimator. Randomised evaluations of deployed AI tools [@peng2023copilot; @becker2025metr; @bean2026llmmedical] randomise people or tasks, which presumes no interference; a store shared by a fleet violates that.

**Online controlled experiments.** The unit of randomisation here is the fleet epoch because treated and control units would share state [@blake2014marketplace; @johari2022twosided; @saveski2017network]; the relevant designs are switchbacks [@bojinov2023switchback; @hu2022switchback; @basse2023minimax] with randomisation inference [@bojinov2019timeseries]. We fixed a two-hour washout ex ante instead of estimating the carryover order, have 20 periods, and did not interleave [@radlinski2008clickthrough; @hofmann2016online]. With nine to eleven clusters our percentile cluster bootstrap is in the regime where such intervals under-cover [@cameron2008bootstrap; @webb2014reworking; @cameron2015practitioner]; the registered re-randomisation test is the inference to weight. Field experiments with rare, noisy outcomes are routinely under-powered [@lewis2015unfavorable]; ours is a weaker case, because the sample size ignored a 30-day eligibility window.

**Pre-registration.** Pre-registration has been piloted in ML and NLP [@bertinetto2020prereg; @albanie2022prereg; @vanmiltenburg2021prereg; @sogaard2023twosided], argued for agent experiments, where memory settings are a listed researcher degree of freedom [@vaccaro2026prereg], and recommended for IR as results-blind review [@bauer2023dagstuhl]. The only memory-specific pre-registered design we found is a benchmark study with six pre-registered gates [@feng2026memorytransplants]. This trial is a registration, not a registered report, and its protocol was never peer-reviewed before data. Registered outcomes have been associated with more nulls in large clinical trials [@kaplan2015nullnhlbi], which is the background for publishing an under-powered one.

We found no pre-registered randomised memory trial on live traffic published before this one; the search was bounded and the most relevant work is two days old.
